source.title: Beyond Top Activations: Efficient and Reliable Crowdsourced Evaluation of Automated Interpretability
source.authors: Tuomas P. Oikarinen; Ge Yan; Akshay R. Kulkarni; T. Weng

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates vision-neuron explanations against activations across full or held-out image data using correlation, a different measure from the original audit. This bears on V6’s concern that descriptions based on activating examples may not predict neuron activity more broadly.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates explanation quality, not the proportion of neuron poles with one or more jobs. It reports correlation scores for descriptions and simulated activation predictions. Its discussion that focusing on highly activating inputs can yield overly specific explanations is relevant to V6. The study uses images and vision models, not language-model neurons or text.
record.test_reason: The study scores vision-neuron explanations by correlation over the full ImageNet validation set, not only top-activating inputs. Methods that describe top activations (ND, MILAN, DnD, MAIA, Compositional Explanations) score low (about 0.02–0.15). The authors attribute this partly to explanations being 'overly specific' and missing lower activations. That bears on V6, though in vision models rather than language models. The study does not measure share of neurons interpretable (V1, V2, V4), circuits (V5) or text simulation (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main contribution is MG-IS and BRAgg, which cut crowdsourced evaluation cost about 40× (from about $90,000 to $2,160). The large-scale study then finds Linear Explanations best, with LLM-based methods (DnD, MAIA) not beating simpler baselines. Overall correlations are low (best about 0.2), which the authors attribute to top-activation focus and inconsistency.
record.recipe_differences: This is a vision-neuron explanation evaluation using correlation between neuron activations and concept-presence labels, including crowdsourced ratings and SigLIP-based simulated predictions; it does not reproduce the neuron-pole audit.
record.method_sensitivity: Scores vary by model/layer, explanation method, explanation complexity, and rating aggregation prior. In the large-scale crowdsourced comparison, the authors report different method rankings by model and aggregation; they also report higher average scores for ViT-B-16 than ResNet-50 in some examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Vision analogue of V7: simulation-with-correlation scoring of vision-neuron explanations, using SigLIP predicted concept presence on unseen images, gives low mean scores for every method. The best is LE at 0.24–0.38, and humans rate the best methods about 0.2. Linear Explanations score best overall.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ImageNet vision models' last layers, simulation-scored neuron explanations reach only low mean correlations (≤0.38) for all tested methods, with full-range Linear Explanations best.

record.problems: The study focuses on two ImageNet-trained vision models and selected layers, not language models. The large-scale study evaluates 100 randomly selected neurons per model and method. Crowdsourced ratings have low inter-annotator agreement: Fleiss’s Kappa 0.191 on ViT explanations and 0.274 on ResNet-50 explanations. Some automated Table 1 and Table 2 averages use subsets for specified methods. Aggregate correlations do not report the fraction of neurons above a threshold for a good explanation.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports more than 60 results if all MG-IS/BRAgg validation simulations, sampling ablations, and human-study results are included. Kept the neuron-explanation quality scores most relevant to V6: Table 1 and Table 2 automated correlation scores and Table 4/Table 3 crowdsourced correlations. Left out sampling-cost/error results in Figures 2–13 and validation-setting RCE results in Sections 3–4 because they evaluate the proposed evaluation pipeline’s accuracy/cost rather than explanation quality itself. Table 3 has 10 rows; only the ResNet-50 entries are included here due to the 60-row cap.

untested.parts: All: no audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles.
All: no language models and no share of interpretable neurons.
All: no InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
Compares explanation tools but reports no share of interpretable neurons, and no architecture or regularization manipulation.
All: no circuits or attribution graphs.
Language-model neurons on text. It also never measures how well explanations fit the activating examples themselves; only full-distribution correlation is reported.
Text simulation for language-model neurons, a fraction of neurons above a good-score threshold, and explainer-strength comparison.

missing.what: Table 3 (SigLIP 2 prior) entries for ResNet-50 DnD 0.1242, MAIA 0.1072 and LE 0.1786, and all ViT-B-16 entries (LE 0.2591, MAIA 0.1355, DnD 0.1039, etc.)

Per-neuron examples: no ResNet-50 neuron scored very high (the authors call these neurons densely activated and polysemantic), while several ViT neurons exceeded 0.5 (e.g. neuron 2187, ibex). MAIA sometimes gives the best explanation.
Significance tests of LE versus top-activation methods: p-values for LE>DnD and LE>MAIA

record.verdict_notes: Linked V6 rows only where the method derives explanations from top-activating inputs; full-range methods (CD, INVERT, CCE, LE) are comparators set to none. The setting is vision, not language, and fit to the activating examples is never measured directly. Low ViT scores for 2d-designed methods may be partly an artefact of broadcasting scalar activations. Inter-rater agreement is low (Fleiss's kappa 0.19–0.27).

versions.untested_parts: The share of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one or more jobs and the share not understood.
Interpretability shares across language models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, and recursive generalization.
Whether architecture, regularization, and tools explain interpretability rates, including the InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model.
The study does not isolate explanations’ fit to the exact activating examples used to write them, and it tests vision models on images rather than language models on text.
It does not report what fraction of neurons exceed a good-score threshold on new text, or compare explainer model strength as stated in this version.

source_check.notes: The automated scores (Tables 1–2) are SigLIP-simulated on a 10,000-input test split. The human scores cover 100 random neurons per model, estimated by MG-IS over the full ImageNet val. Authors attribute the low ND/CompExp scores to Broden concept sets, and ViT scores for 2d methods may be depressed by activation broadcasting (C.3.1). The 'top-activation focus' reason is given for LLM methods not beating simpler baselines, not for the overall low scores.

statements.correction: Table 1/2 (SigLIP-simulated correlation on a 10,000-input test split, RN-50/ViT-B-16): ND 0.1242/0.0335, MILAN 0.0920/0.0194, DnD 0.1534/0.1049, MAIA 0.1396/0.1497 (100 neurons), CompExp l=3 0.1399/0.0468, CD 0.1904/0.1849, INVERT 0.1867/0.1343, LE(SigLIP) l=1 0.2413/0.2968. Authors: LE is the only tested method optimized for the entire activation range. They attribute the low Broden-based (ND, CompExp) scores to concept sets lacking higher-level concepts.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the automated scores are not computed over the full ImageNet validation set: they use a 10,000-input test split. The 0.02–0.15 range also leaves out CD and INVERT, which the study does not count as full-range (it names only LE).

statements.correction: RN-50 Layer4, 100 random neurons: majority DnD 0.0978, CD 0.0978, LE 0.1216. BRAgg uniform: DnD 0.1011, CD 0.1017, LE 0.1261 (LE>DnD p=0.0198; LE>CD p=0.0601). The authors call LE the only method optimized for the full activation range. This bears on V6 as support.
statements.problem: The numbers are right but the reading is wrong. The study does not treat CD as full-range: LE is the only full-range method tested. LE still beats DnD under both aggregations, so these results do not show the shortfall is non-specific.

statements.correction: The study calls LE the only tested method optimized for the entire activation range. Human-rated RN-50 CD scores are 0.0978 (majority), 0.1017 (BRAgg uniform) and 0.1356 (BRAgg SigLIP). DnD scores 0.0978, 0.1011 and 0.1179.
statements.problem: The CD numbers are right. The stated disagreement between verdicts rests on 2506.07985's verdict calling CD full-range, which the study's text does not support. The study agrees that CD is not full-range.

reader_labels.condition: Evaluated simple and complex explanations for ResNet-50 Layer4 and ViT-B-16 Layer11 MLP neurons
reader_labels.reason: Full-distribution or held-out activation correlation scores are often modest; the authors also conclude that focusing on highly activating inputs can produce overly specific descriptions that miss lower activations. See r01-r28 and r29-r58.
